materials.text: Made belongings, food and gifts participate in social responsibilities; they are more than interchangeable decorations.

knowledge.text: Witnesses, names and responsibilities give the ceremony significance that a ban did not erase.

citations.locator: Barb Cranmer transcript: Potlatch Means to Give

custody.text: Government publications, confiscation records and community-directed return expose different forms of authority over collections.

name: Kwakwaka’wakw potlatch: witnesses, prohibition and return
place: Northern Vancouver Island and adjacent mainland; locator at Alert Bay
geographicPrecision: Alert Bay is a cultural-center locator, not a border or a claim that every Kwakwaka’wakw nation shares one origin. 1921’s potlatch took place at Village Island.

interval.label: Selected legislation and cultural-center history, 1884–1980
interval.note: The 1884 legislation, effective in 1885, and 1980 opening of U’mista frame this inquiry, not the existence of potlatch or the end of return efforts. Prohibition was removed in 1951; practices continued during it. Later returns are not projected backward into 1980.

question: Can a government ban a practice without ending its authority for a community?
summary: In the public Kwakwaka’wakw accounts selected here, guests witness consequential family events, while preparation, food and gifts make responsibilities visible. Canadian prohibition attacked these relationships. Particular recollections and return histories explain why a law, a museum’s custody and a community’s authority are different forms of evidence.

sections.title: Preparation supports people who witness
sections.text: A potlatch requires work before invited people arrive. The AMNH presentation, made with Kwakwaka’wakw contributors, describes extended families gathering food and gifts. Guests help verify claims about family history and inherited standing; gifts acknowledge their presence as witnesses. U’mista describes events including naming, marriage, leadership and death. This makes preparation consequential social work, rather than an unexplained pile of possessions. The public accounts give an entry into these responsibilities without turning every Northwest Coast nation’s institutions into one identical practice.

citations.locator: P’a̱sa: preparation, witnesses and family work

sections.title: Prohibition changed the risks of participation
sections.text: U’mista distinguishes the 1884 amendment from the law taking effect on 1 January 1885. Continued potlatching shows that government prohibition did not erase community authority. After Dan Cranmer’s 1921 gathering at Village Island, prosecutions and confiscations followed. The pressure reached families and their belongings. In the public Impact transcript, Vera Newman recalls fear and a family’s experience of imprisonment. Chief Bill Cranmer explains the pressure to surrender belongings to keep members from jail. These are particular accounts, not a single experience assigned to everyone.

citations.locator: Impact transcript; named Vera Newman and Chief Bill Cranmer captions; Start

sections.title: Return required organization and family decisions
sections.text: Removing the prohibition in 1951 did not bring the belongings home automatically. U’mista’s history names Chief Jimmy Sewid and band councils among those pursuing return. Meetings involved Elders and representatives, and negotiations addressed where treasures would be cared for. The history says oldest living descendants of original owners were to decide where their belongings would be held. The return account describes planning museums at Alert Bay and Cape Mudge. Building institutions was part of sustained work to recover care and decision-making.

sections.title: A returned belonging has a particular history
sections.text: U’mista opened in 1980, the endpoint of the original case. Its public captions connect returned belongings with named relatives, including Florence Matilpi and her grandson Sean with a headdress belonging to her grandfather. Another caption records a 2003 headdress return connected with Chief Sam Scow. These accounts extend beyond an anonymous museum category. They do not establish every missing link in custody or imply that all belongings returned by 1980. Continuing community knowledge also exceeds what the old title page can tell us.

claims.text: The 1884 legislation did not end potlatching; U’mista documents continuing practice, confiscations following the 1921 potlatch and the 1951 removal of the prohibition.

returnPrompt: What is the difference between a law prohibiting a ceremony, evidence that people continued it, and a community deciding where belongings should be kept?

deeperReading.title: A publication credit and a community account answer different questions
deeperReading.text: The existing title page names George Hunt’s collected data and Franz Boas’s authorship. Its publication date is 1921, while the annual report covers 1913–14. Reading those credits is useful evidence of how the publication represents its making. It cannot show every conversation, contributor or obligation behind the knowledge. It also does not document the Village Island gathering merely because the dates overlap. Read it beside the attributed community accounts rather than allowing a government imprint to decide whose interpretation counts.

citations.locator: Named project team, film-maker and educational/language consultants

deeperReading.title: Care after return is more than a change of address
deeperReading.text: The return transcript explains that museum construction was made a condition of returning part of the collection. It also describes the community’s choices about how belongings should be housed, including why some contributors opposed locking them into cases again. That explanation belongs to a particular public account; it does not grant visitors unrestricted access to every meaning or ceremony. A named caption can connect a returned treasure with a family, while still leaving parts of its history uncertain. The Agnes Alfred caption, for example, gives grandfather or uncle as alternative relationships. Keeping that uncertainty is more useful than inventing a complete biography. Public study can examine these records without copying a ceremonial image or asking a family to perform someone else’s responsibilities.

evidenceReading.title: Witnessing, published credit and the work of return
evidenceReading.introduction: A legal milestone, a public family recollection, a title-page credit and a return caption support different kinds of claims. None replaces all the others.

items.label: A particular speaker explains the pressure
items.text: U’mista’s Impact page names Vera Newman and Chief Bill Cranmer beside statements about fear, family imprisonment and surrender under pressure.
items.interpretation: Attribute their accounts and identify their retrospective setting. They explain consequences that a date of legislation cannot show; they are not a census of every family’s experience.

items.label: A printed attribution is evidence of published credit
items.text: The title page names Hunt’s data and Boas’s authorship; the old report period and 1921 publication are distinct.
items.interpretation: This page establishes what the publication credits. It does not show the 1921 potlatch, recover every contributor or confer exclusive authority over community knowledge.

citations.locator: Retained ethnographic and annual-report title pages

items.label: A return caption locates a particular family history
items.text: U’mista identifies Florence and Sean Matilpi with a returned headdress in 1980 and separately records the 2003 return associated with Sam Scow.
items.interpretation: Keep each identified relationship, represented date and source role distinct. These captions are not a complete collection inventory, permission to reproduce every image or proof all restitution was finished.

familyActivity.title: Read the page and separate the claim
steps: Find George Hunt and Franz Boas on the supplied title page, then compare the different words used for their roles.
Read the capsule and distinguish the publication year from the report period.
Write a claim the page supports about credit, followed by a question it cannot answer about a community event or contributor.
Read one attributed community account in the dossier. Explain what it adds without pretending that you witnessed the historical event or performing a ceremony.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: The title page identifies George Hunt’s collected data and names Franz Boas as author. It was published in 1921; the annual-report period 1913–14 is a separate date. These credits show how the publication presents its sources. The page does not show Dan Cranmer’s potlatch, identify every contributor or supply permission to repeat a ceremony.

review.reviewer: Codex selected public source consultation and internal author QA; not independent Kwakwaka’wakw/community or historian acceptance
review.scope: Family preparation and witnesses; particular public recollections of pressure and confiscation; community-directed care and named return accounts. Two new records and four selected dated renewals retain all preceding scopes. The old Hunt/Boas record remains at its prior title-page consultation because current LOC access returned 403. Exact original case identity, complete 1884–1980 interval/note, claims/dimensions/terms and all media fields/bytes are preserved. No new media, annotation, placeStudy, route or historical relationship added.
limitations: Selected public English text/transcripts and source captions were consulted; no original film/audio played, original court/negotiation files inspected, full ethnography read or private family testimony obtained. A 2026 copyright footer does not date the film or photograph.

U’mista’s pages give inconsistent imprisonment totals. No count is adopted or silently harmonized. Named speakers’ retrospective accounts do not become identical experiences or approval by all Kwakwaka’wakw nations.

The actual existing title-page pixels were viewed unchanged. LOC’s current catalogue returned 403; its prior 27 October consultation is retained, not newly dated. The page is a printed document, not a photograph of confiscation, and its historic title is not a universal name for the peoples.

Source captions, not original photographic pixels, establish the selected 1980 and 2003 return examples. No new ceremonial image is downloaded or reproduced. No complete chain of custody or current outstanding return total is claimed.
The wider reference reaches a particular 2003 return account while the original case ends in 1980. Neither endpoint dates potlatch’s origin, end of community authority or completion of every return.

Public introductory teaching and copyright status do not authorize reproducing restricted ceremony, songs, stories or meanings. This account does not supply reenactment instructions or unrestricted visual rights. Independent community/historian review and integrated family, screen-reader/device and physical-print acceptance remain open.
